summary: Specifies a fast reroute framework for protecting services and tunnels against egress node and link failures. It defines roles such as point of local repair, protector, and backup egress, and describes how a bypass tunnel and context-based forwarding reduce traffic loss before the network converges.

eli5.summary: If the last stop on a bus line is closed, a backup stop nearby can take passengers right away while the planners work out a new plan.

questions: what is a protector in mpls fast reroute
what is a context id in mpls
subtitle: How MPLS networks keep carrying traffic for a customer site when the last router or link on the path fails.

tldr.problem: When the egress router of an MPLS tunnel, or its link to the customer, fails, traffic is lost until control-plane convergence or global repair catches up.
tldr.mechanism: The router just before the failure (the PLR) pre-builds a bypass tunnel to a protector router that already hosts backup service instances. When the failure is detected, the PLR switches traffic onto the bypass, and the protector uses a context label to forward each packet using the failed router's own labels.
tldr.outcome: Local repair gives a fast but temporary fix, and the RFC says it is RECOMMENDED to use it together with control-plane convergence or global repair, which provide the permanent fix.

today: RFC 8679 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2019, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework: specific protocol details are left to separate documents, such as the RSVP-TE extensions in RFC 8400.

sections.title: Protecting the Last Hop of a Tunnel
sections.content:
MPLS networks use Label Switched Paths (LSPs) as transport tunnels that carry services such as Layer 2 VPNs and Layer 3 VPNs. The egress router of a tunnel hosts the service instances and forwards service packets over an egress link (often called a PE-CE link or attachment circuit) to the service destination, using a service label.

Local-repair fast reroute was already used for transit link and node failures, with restoration times in the order of tens of milliseconds. A router upstream of the failure, the Point of Local Repair (PLR), pre-builds a bypass tunnel to a Merge Point and switches to it when the failure is detected locally. RFC 8679 extends this idea to failures of the egress node and the egress link.

The framework requires that the destination of a service MUST be dual-homed, or have dual paths into the MPLS network, via two edge routers. It does not require extensions to RSVP, LDP or BGP for the tunnels themselves, although it gives guidelines for extensions to IGPs and service label distribution protocols.

Services with upstream-assigned service labels, and broadcast, multicast and unknown unicast traffic in VPLS and EVPN, are left for future study.
sections.eli5: Imagine a package route where the last delivery truck breaks down. This RFC says a nearby helper should already know the way to the customer's house, so packages can be handed over at once.

sections.title: Roles and Vocabulary
sections.content:
The framework defines several roles. The egress router is the tunnel's tail end and hosts the service instances. The PLR is the penultimate hop router in egress node protection, and the egress router itself in egress link protection. The backup egress router is another router that can also reach the service destinations and hosts a backup service instance.

The protector is the router that acts as an alternate for the protected egress router. It hosts a protection service instance for each protected service and is the tail end of the bypass tunnel. In the co-located protector mode the protector is the backup egress router. In the centralized protector mode the protector is a dedicated router decoupled from the backup egress routers.

A protected egress {E, P} is a virtual node made of the egress router E and its protector P. A context ID is a globally unique IP address assigned to it, and a context label is a non-reserved label that the protector assigns to that context ID.
sections.eli5: Think of a relay team. One runner finishes the race, a spare runner stands ready, and a teammate just before the finish line hands the baton to the spare if the first runner trips.

sections.title: Detection, Protectors and the Context ID
sections.content:
The PLR detects an egress node failure through a node liveness mechanism or from the collective failure of all links to that node. The detection MUST be reasonably fast, meaning faster than control-plane failure detection and remote failure detection, or local repair has little benefit. If the PLR can tell a link failure from a node failure, it SHOULD set up both link protection and egress node protection and trigger only one of them.

A tunnel is protected by only one protector, but a protector may protect several tunnels and several egress routers. The protector MUST have its own connectivity to each service destination, and that connectivity MUST NOT traverse the protected egress router.

The context ID ties everything together. It is an IPv4 or IPv6 address logically owned by both the egress router and the protector. The egress router attaches it to service label bindings or IP service advertisements, the ingress router uses it as the destination of the egress-protected tunnel, and the PLR uses it as the destination of the bypass tunnel while avoiding the egress router. The protector keeps a dedicated label space and IP address space for each egress router, and the context label identifies them.
sections.eli5: The context ID is like a shared mailbox name that both the main post office and the backup post office answer to. Everyone writes the same name on the parcel, and only the backup knows how to sort it if the main office is shut.

sections.title: Advertising the Context ID
sections.content:
Egress router E and protector P MUST coordinate how the context ID is reachable in the routing and TE domains, so that egress-protected tunnels end at E and bypass tunnels end at P while avoiding E. The RFC suggests three approaches and treats them as technically equal:

  • Proxy mode: E and P advertise the context ID as a virtual proxy node connected to both, with the link to E having a more preferable IGP and TE metric. The PLR does not need to know the egress protection schema.
  • Alias mode: E simply advertises the context ID as an IP address, and P advertises the context ID and context label in a "context ID label binding" advertisement, defined as the IGP Mirroring Context segment in RFC 8402 and RFC 8667. E does not need to know the schema.
  • Stub link mode: E and P both advertise the context ID as a link to a stub network, like an anycast address. Care MUST be taken about whether this approach applies to a network.

All relevant routers, including the primary PE, the protector and the PLR, MUST support and agree on the chosen approach. This can be done by configuration.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to tell the road map about the shared mailbox name. Whichever way a town picks, everyone in that town has to use the same one.

sections.title: Bypass Tunnels and Local Repair
sections.content:
The PLR sets up an egress-protection bypass tunnel to the context ID while avoiding the egress router, using constraint-based computation similar to that used for traffic engineering paths and Loop-Free Alternate (LFA) paths. The tunnel may be built by a signaling protocol such as RSVP, by a topology-driven protocol such as LDP, or hierarchically, with the context label as a one-hop LSP over a regular bypass tunnel to the protector. Segment Routing can also be used, with the context label as the inner-most SID label. In every case the bypass is an ultimate hop-popping tunnel whose incoming label on P is the context label.

The PLR is agnostic to services and service labels. It keeps bypass state per transport tunnel, not per service, and may share one bypass tunnel among several egress-protected tunnels with the same protected egress. During repair it reroutes all packets from the protected tunnels onto the bypass and leaves service labels intact. Depending on the bypass type, it swaps the incoming label to the bypass label, or swaps to the context label and pushes the label or label stack of the regular bypass.

At the protector, the context label is popped first. For an MPLS service packet, P then looks up the service label in E's label space (context label switching). For an IP service packet it looks up the destination address in E's IP address space (context IP forwarding). To make this work, there MUST be a service label distribution session between each egress router and the protector, so the protector learns the egress router's service labels.
sections.eli5: The helper just before the broken stop already has a side road marked to the backup stop. When the main stop closes, every parcel goes down that road with its original label still on it, and the backup stop reads that label using the main stop's own sorting book.

sections.title: Centralized Mode and Egress Link Protection
sections.content:
In centralized protector mode a small number of dedicated protectors each protect a subset of egress routers. The protector cannot send packets straight to the service destination, so it MUST send them over another transport tunnel to the backup service instance on a backup egress router. For an MPLS service, it MUST swap the service label to the label of the backup service and push the transport tunnel label or labels. The backup egress router can reuse the label it gave to ingress routers only if that label's forwarding state does not point towards the protected egress router, because otherwise the packets would loop. If it does, the backup egress router MUST advertise a unique label for egress protection.

For egress link protection the egress router itself acts as the PLR and pre-establishes a bypass tunnel to the protector. There are two approaches. In the first, the egress router does not know the backup egress router's service label, so it pushes the bypass label and keeps its own service label. The protector MUST then perform context label switching, and both protector modes are supported. In the second, the egress router knows the backup service label through a label distribution session. It swaps to that label and pushes the bypass label, and the bypass tunnel goes to an ordinary address of the protector instead of the context ID. Only the co-located mode applies to this second approach.

Protection for an ingress link failure in the opposite direction of a bidirectional service SHOULD come from a separate mechanism and is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the spare helper is only a sorting hub, and it has to pass parcels on to yet another shop. In that case it swaps each parcel's sticker for the one that last shop expects.

sections.title: Worked Example: Layer 3 VPN Egress Protection
sections.content:
The RFC's example has site 1 attached to PE1 and site 2 dual-homed to PE2 and PE3. PE2 is the primary PE for site 2 and PE3 is the protector in co-located mode, forming protected egress {PE2, PE3} with context ID 198.51.100.1. PE3 assigns context label 100 and creates a label table pe2.mpls to represent PE2's label space. The core uses OSPF and RSVP-TE, and PE2 and PE3 use proxy mode to advertise the context ID.

PE2 allocates labels per VRF: 9000 for IPv4 and 9001 for IPv6. It advertises site 2's prefixes by BGP with those labels and next hop 198.51.100.1. PE1 signals an RSVP tunnel to the context ID with the "node protection desired" flag set. PE3, seeing the context ID, installs labels 9000 and 9001 in pe2.mpls and points them at protection VRFs built from PE3's own connectivity to site 2.

R1, the penultimate hop, is the PLR. It computes the bypass path R1-R2-PE3 and signals it. When R1 detects PE2 failing, packets reach PE3 with outer label 100 and inner label 9000 or 9001. PE3 pops the context label, looks up the VPN label in pe2.mpls, pops it and forwards to site 2. For link failure, PE2 swaps to PE3's own labels 10000 and 10001 and pushes the bypass label. Eventually global repair makes PE1 choose PE3 as the new entrance to site 2.
sections.eli5: In the example, a company site has two doors. If the main door fails, the guard just before it sends visitors along a side corridor to the second door, and the second door's guard uses the first door's guest list to let them in.

sections.title: Global Repair and Security
sections.content:
The framework gives a fast but temporary repair. For permanent repair, affected services SHOULD be moved to an alternative tunnel or replaced by alternative services, which is called global repair. It can be triggered by control-plane notifications, end-to-end OAM and fault detection, among others. A PLR SHOULD also generate an alert when it performs local repair.

The security section says the framework needs a service label distribution protocol between an egress router and a protector over a secure session, and that the security properties depend entirely on the underlying protocol. If the PLR, protector and backup egress router are not in the same administrative domain, a certain level of trust MUST be established between them. The document concludes it introduces no new security threat.

One concern it names is an attacker controlling a CE who simulates link failures to trigger cascading activity. As a general defence, the egress router SHOULD use a damping mechanism to suppress the services associated with the link or CE. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The backup plan is a quick patch, and the town still has to fix the road for good. Also, if a trouble-maker keeps pretending the road is broken, the road crew should stop listening to that person for a while.
